I. INTRODUCTION

This technical description (TD) is intended for the study of the KM1801VM2 integrated circuit.

Symbols and abbreviations used in this TD are given in Appendix 1.

The instruction set is given in Appendix 2.

[Green Text]
Hereafter in the text, wherever the KM1801VM2
integrated circuit type is mentioned,
it shall also be understood to apply to the KR1801VM2.

2. PURPOSE

2.1. The KM1801VM2 integrated circuit is a single-chip 16-bit microprocessor
(hereinafter referred to as the CPU) intended for processing digital information.

As part of a computer system, the CPU may be used for controlling technological
processes, in instrumentation and measurement equipment, in communication
systems, and for solving engineering, technical, and economic problems.

2.2. Operating Conditions
The integrated circuit can withstand mechanical stresses in accordance with
GOST 18725-73:
    vibration loads in the frequency range 1–600 Hz with a maximum
    acceleration of 98 m/s² (10 g);
    repeated shocks with a maximum acceleration of 735 m/s² (75 g),
    shock duration 2–6 ms;
    single shocks with a maximum acceleration of 1470 m/s² (150 g),
    shock duration 1–3 ms;
    linear centrifugal loads with a maximum acceleration of
    245 m/s² (25 g).

Operation of the integrated circuit is permitted under the following climatic
conditions in accordance with GOST 18725-73:
    maximum ambient temperature: +70°C;
    minimum ambient temperature: −10°C;
    repeated cyclic temperature changes from −10°C to +70°C;
    maximum relative air humidity of 98% at a temperature of +35°C,
    without moisture condensation.
pages.notes:
ПРЦ is an abbreviation for процессор ("processor"). Since this document consistently uses the abbreviation, translating it as CPU is natural and matches PDP-11 terminology.

технологические процессы is the standard Soviet phrase for industrial/process-control applications.

The environmental specifications are characteristic of the commercial/industrial grade KM1801VM2, not the later military-temperature variants.

The handwritten note above the title again changes КМ1801ВМ2 to КР1801ВМ2, consistent with the editorial corrections seen on previous pages.

2.3. The minimum operating life of the integrated circuit under the specified
operating modes and conditions is not less than 15,000 hours. The failure rate
during operation is 0.9 × 10⁻⁶ failures per hour.

2.4. The CPU is powered from a single supply voltage source of:
    +5 V ±5%.
pages.notes:
The stated failure rate corresponds to 0.9 failures per million device-hours.

Интенсивность отказов literally means "failure intensity"; in English reliability specifications this is normally rendered as failure rate.

Наработка is a reliability-engineering term. "Operating life" is the most natural translation here, although "service life" or "mean accumulated operating time" are sometimes used.

3. TECHNICAL DATA

3.1. The CPU is manufactured using P-channel MOS technology. The die,
containing approximately 120 thousand elements, has dimensions of
5.3 × 5.45 mm and is housed in a 40-pin metal-ceramic DIP package,
type 2123.40-6, UФ0.487.024 TU. The conventional schematic symbol
of the CPU is shown in Fig. 1.

3.2. The number system for data and instructions is binary.
3.3. Data and instruction word length is 16 binary bits.

3.4. The instruction set includes zero-address, one-address, and two-address instructions.

3.5. Addressing modes:
    register,
    register indirect,
    autoincrement,
    indirect autoincrement,
    autodecrement,
    indirect autodecrement,
    indexed,
    indirect indexed.

3.6. Number of general-purpose registers: 8.
3.7. Number of information transfer channels: 1.
3.8. Number of interrupt request levels: 2.
    Processing of external and internal interrupts is performed using stack-type memory (the stack).
3.9. Number of instructions: 77.
3.10. Addressable memory capacity: 128 Kbytes
(user programs: 64 Kbytes).

3.11. Clock frequency:
    0–10 MHz (Group A),
    0–8 MHz  (Group B).

3.12. Execution time of an ADD instruction using register addressing at a clock frequency of 10 MHz: 1.0 μs.
pages.notes: The addressing modes listed are exactly the eight standard PDP-11 addressing modes.

4. DESCRIPTION OF CPU PINS

The electrical circuits of the CPU input and output elements are shown in
Figures 2–6. The designations and names of the pins are given in Table 2.

Pins 09–02, 39–32 — AD (0–15)

Sixteen input/output lines of the system bus multiplexed for addresses and
data. They are intended for transmitting and receiving addresses and data.
The use of the same pins for both address and data transfer is achieved by
time multiplexing. A low signal level on these pins corresponds to the
transmission of a logical one.

Pin 10 - Reserved output.
Pin 11 - Reserved input.

Pin 12 — "DMR"
DMA request signal input. This signal (active low) is asserted by an external
device on the system bus to indicate that it requires direct access to memory.

Pin 13 — "SACK"
DMA grant acknowledge signal input. This signal (active low) is asserted by
the device that requested DMA after it receives the DMA grant signal and
indicates that bus control has been transferred to that device.

Pin 14 — "DMGO"
DMA grant signal output. This signal (active low) is asserted by the CPU in
response to receipt of the DMR signal, indicating that direct memory access
has been granted.

Pin 15. "CLCO" (Clock Output)
Output of the chip’s internal clock signal. Used 
to synchronize devices operating with the CPU. The pulse 
frequency of CL CO is equal to half the pulse frequency of CLCI.

Pin 16. "CLCI" (Clock Input)
Input of the clock pulse signal. This signal is used
to synchronize the operation of the PRC’s internal devices.
The microcircuit consists of static-type devices.
Therefore, the clock frequency can be from 0 to 10 MHz.

Pin 17. "~RPLY" (Reply)
Input of the response signal of the slave device during an exchange.
This signal is asserted by the slave device during exchanges over the system
bus, informing the master device that it has accepted
or delivered information to the system bus.

Pin 18. "~DOUT" (Data Out Strobe)
Output of the write strobe signal during the exchange procedure
over the system bus. By asserting a low level signal
on this pin, the CPU informs the slave device that data
have been placed on the system bus.

Pin 19. "~WTBT" (Write Byte)
Output of the combined informational signal "write-byte"
During address output in the exchange procedure cycle over the system
bus, a low level on this pin indicates that a write procedure is being performed. During data output, a low level on this pin indicates
that a byte rather than a word is being output.

Pin 20. "0V" (GND)
Common output (ground) for all CPU devices, except for the AD (0–15) and SEL signal amplifiers.

Pin 21. "~SYNC"
Exchange synchronization signal output.
By setting a low signal level on this pin, the CPU informs
the slave device that the address has been placed on the system bus.

Pin 22. "~DIN"
Data read procedure signal output. By setting a low
signal level on this pin, the CPU informs the slave device
that it is ready to receive data from the system bus.

Pin 23. "~AR"
Address Accepted signal input. After issuing an address
onto the system bus and asserting the SYNC signal,
the CPU waits for the AR signal. A low signal level on this pin indicates
that the slave device has accepted the address and the CPU may continue the exchange procedure.

Pin 24. "~IAKO"
Interrupt acknowledge signal output. A low signal level on this
pin indicates that the CPU permits the device that asserted the
interrupt request to place the interrupt vector onto the system bus.

Pin 25. "~ACLO"
Mains power failure signal input. A transition of the signal from high
to low level on this pin causes a CPU interrupt and transfers execution to
the power-failure interrupt service routine. A high signal level on this
pin indicates normal mains power conditions and causes transition
to the execution of the microprogram start-up.

Pin 26. "~DCLO"
Power supply failure signal input. A low level of the signal on this pin causes initialization
of all blocks of the microcircuit and the appearance of the "set" signal on pin "~INIT".

Pin 27. "~INIT"
Set signal output. This signal is used for initializing the peripheral part of the system.
This signal duplicates the DCLO signal

Pin 28. "~VIRQ"
Vector interrupt request signal input.
When a low level of the CPU signal appears on this pin, if interrupts are
enabled, outputs the signals "~DIN" & "~TAKO".

Pin 29. "~HALT"
Console mode entry signal input.
The appearance of a low signal level on this pin
causes a transition to the console-mode program located in ROM.

Pin 30. "~EVNT"
Timer interrupt request signal input.
The transition of the signal on this pin from high to low indicates
that the timer has issued an interrupt request.

Pin 31. "~SEL"
System memory area access or port read (initial conditions register) signal output.
The appearance of this signal (low level) in the address output phase indicates
that the exchange is not with the main, but with additional (system) memory.

The appearance of this signal in the read phase simultaneously
with the "~DIN" signal (low level) indicates that the CPU is performing
the procedure for reading the initial-conditions register.

Note: A low level must be applied to pin "~SP2" (pin II).
Note: For processor operation on the system bus using "~SP1" and "~SP2" signals, see Chapter 12 of this Technical Description (TO).

5. DESCRIPTION OF THE STRUCTURAL DIAGRAM OF THE CPU

5.1. The general structural diagram of the PRC is shown in Fig.7.

The CPU consists of the following blocks:
    Operational block (OB);
    Microprogram control block (BMU);
    Extended arithmetic block (BRA);
    Interrupt block (BPR);
    Branch condition processing block (BOV);
    Interface block (IB).

Via the internal address-data bus, data and instructions are supplied to the OB,
and instructions to the BOV and BMU. On this same bus, the OB outputs operand addresses.

Through interface elements, the internal bus is connected to the AD pins and through them to the system bus.

The BMU outputs the microinstruction code onto the microinstruction bus.
From the microinstruction bus, the corresponding fields of the microinstruction are supplied
to all CPU blocks except the BOV.

In addition, the blocks are interconnected by synchronous and asynchronous control signals.

The OB is the leading block. The OB synchronization block monitors,
directly or indirectly, the state of all groups of blocks and sets the execution cycle
of the microinstructions that make up an instruction.

5.2. Operational block
The structural diagram of the operational block (OB) is shown in Fig.8.
The OB is intended to perform the following functions:
  Address calculation and its temporary storage in the address register;

Figure 7. Structural Diagram of the KM1801VM2 Integrated Circuit

A copy of the Program Counter (PC Copy Register, PCRC) and a comparator
(COMP) have been added to the instruction-word processing path. The PCRC
stores the address of the word following the instruction, i.e., PC + 2.

Before a write cycle, the address on the Address Register (AR) is compared
by the comparator with the contents of the PCRC. If they are equal, then
after completion of the write cycle the instruction stored at the address
contained in the PCRC is read. In other words, the next instruction is
fetched again. The previously fetched next instruction is not executed.
This repeated-read procedure is implemented by hardware microprogram control.

In some instructions, the low-order byte of the instruction is used to
calculate an address. For receiving this byte, the BRK OB and RK OB
registers are used. The low-order byte of the instruction being executed
is stored in RK OB.

The Constant Block is used to generate constants required for execution
of certain operations and for generating interrupt vectors. The Constant
Block is implemented as a ROM whose cell addresses are contained in a
special field of the microinstruction. The instruction displacement code
is also read from the constant address. For this purpose, the code of the
low-order byte of the instruction is supplied to the Constant Block.

For selecting interrupt vectors, the interrupt vector address generated
by the Interrupt Block is also supplied to the Constant Block.

The Processor Status Register and the Status Register Copy Register are
used for storing condition codes (processor states) generated during
execution of operations in the CPU. The format of the Status Register and
the purpose of its individual bits will be described later in the
description of processor operation.

The Status Register Copy Register preserves the contents of the Processor
Status Register during the processing of certain interrupts.

The Execution Unit contains ten registers used for temporary storage of
information. Eight of these are General-Purpose Registers (GPRs). The GPR
with address 07 is used as the Program Counter, and the GPR with address 06
is used as the Stack Pointer.

...stack pointer. These registers may not be used for data storage.

The register block also contains an accumulator and a source register.

The accumulator register is used for temporary storage of information
during execution of certain instructions, while the source register is
used to store the source operand during execution of two-operand
instructions.

The general-purpose registers are accessible by software; the
accumulator and source register are accessible only by microprogram
control.

All arithmetic and logical operations on operands are performed in a
16-bit Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU). The ALU can process both 16-bit
words and 8-bit bytes. The ALU includes a carry-lookahead scheme,
allowing carry propagation through no more than three bit positions
in sequence.

From the ALU, the operation result is sent to the shifter (SHF),
where, during shift instructions, the operand is shifted one bit
position left or right, and the logic for arithmetic and circular
(rotating) shifts is implemented.

Either a 16-bit word or an 8-bit byte may be shifted.

After the shifter, the final result of the operation is obtained and
written into a special register. Writing into this register completes
the read phase of the microinstruction execution cycle.

During the write phase of microinstruction execution, information from
the register holding the operation result passes through the Byte
Exchange Block (BEB) to the Write Circuit (WRC).

In the BEB, the high-order and low-order bytes of an operand are
exchanged when executing the SWAB instruction.

The BEB is also used when outputting the high-order byte during byte
instructions.

All blocks and registers of the Execution Unit are connected by two
buses: the X,Y Read Bus and the X',Y' Write Bus.

During the read phase, information is read onto the X bus or onto the
Y bus in unary operations,

...or simultaneously onto the X and Y buses from different sources during
binary operations, and is then supplied to the ALU.

The write circuitry places information onto the X' and Y' buses, from
which it is routed to the destination address.

By separating the read and write buses, decoding of the read address can
be performed simultaneously with the write cycle, and decoding of the
write address can be performed simultaneously with the read cycle,
thereby reducing the microinstruction execution time.

In addition to the operational section, the Execution Unit (EU) also
contains a microinstruction decoder, a Status Formation Circuit (SFC),
and an Execution Unit Synchronization Block (EUSB).

The fields of the microinstruction related to execution of the
operational portion of the microinstruction—namely operand addresses,
write mode, and operation code—are supplied to the Execution Unit
microinstruction decoder.

After decoding the microinstruction, the control codes are supplied to
the corresponding blocks of the operational section of the Execution
Unit.

Based on signals received from the ALU, the shifter, and the Extended
Arithmetic Block (EAB), the Status Formation Circuit (SFC) generates
the operation result flags N, Z, V, and C, which are stored in the
Processor Status Register (PSR) and subsequently used by branch
instructions.

Operation of the Execution Unit is controlled by the Execution Unit
Synchronization Block (EUSB). The EUSB also synchronizes all other CPU
blocks.

The EUSB monitors the readiness of the Interface Unit (IU) and the
Microprogram Control Unit (MCU).

Upon completion of a microinstruction execution cycle, the EUSB
generates the EU READY signal, which starts the MCU. The MCU then
generates the next microinstruction.

The Interface Unit is started by the signal generated when an address
is written into the Address Register (AR). This signal indicates that
an address has been prepared for output onto the system bus.

5.3. Extended Arithmetic Unit

The structural diagram of the Extended Arithmetic Unit (EAU) is shown
in Figure 9.

The EAU is intended to provide hardware support for execution of the
multiply, divide, and arithmetic shift instructions
(MUL, DIV, ASH, ASHC).

When these instructions are executed, control is transferred to the EAU
after the operands have been fetched.

To execute the main part of the instruction, a single microinstruction
is used. During execution of the operation, this microinstruction is
modified according to a specific algorithm by the EAU control logic.

After completion of the main part of the operation, during multiplication
and division, the microinstruction is changed and result correction and
status generation are performed.

The EAU consists of:
    Extended Arithmetic Register 1 (EAR1);
    Extended Arithmetic Register 2 (EAR2);
    Cycle Counter (CC);
    Cycle Decoder (CD);
    Microinstruction Decoder (MID);
    Control Logic (CL).

EAR1 and EAR2 are used to store intermediate computation results.

EAR2 is a shifting register. During execution of operations it
supplements the ALU shifter.

During multiplication, the multiplier is loaded into EAR2, while
partial products are formed in EAR1.

At the end of the operation, the upper part of the product is contained
in EAR1 and the lower part in EAR2.

During division, the upper part of the dividend is loaded into EAR1
and the lower part into EAR2.

At the end of the operation, the quotient is formed in EAR2 and the
remainder in EAR1.

When performing shift operations, the word being shifted is loaded
into EAR1, or into EAR2 and EAR1 if a double-word operand is being
shifted.

Each EAU instruction is executed in a specific number of clock cycles.
A constant determining the number of cycles is loaded into the Cycle
Counter (CC).

Information from the Cycle Counter is supplied to the Cycle Decoder (CD),
which generates control signals that are sent to the Control Logic (CL).

Based on the instruction code and signals from the Cycle Counter, the
Control Logic implements the algorithm for execution of the operational
part of the instruction, result correction, and condition code generation.

The EAR1, EAR2, and CC registers are addressable by microinstructions.

The address field of the microinstruction is supplied to the
Microinstruction Decoder, where read and write control signals for
these registers are generated under control of signals from the
Operational Unit Synchronization Block.

5.4. Microprogram Control Unit

The structural diagram of the Microprogram Control Unit (MCU) is shown
in Figure 10.

The MCU is intended to generate the sequence of microinstructions
required to execute an instruction based on the received instruction code.

The MCU consists of the following blocks and registers:
    Instruction Buffer Register (IBR);
    Instruction Decoder (ID);
    Instruction Register (IR);
    Microinstruction Memory (MIM);
    Microinstruction Register (MIR);
    Next Address Register (NAR);
    Current Address Register (CAR);
    Interrupt Register (INTR);
    MCU Synchronization Block (MCU-SYNC).

Every instruction received by the processor first enters the Instruction
Buffer Register (IBR).

From the IBR, the instruction is sent to the Instruction Decoder (ID),
where preliminary decoding takes place. The main instruction decoding
function is performed by the decoder PLA. The decoder PLA contains
50 logic product terms. Part of the decoder is implemented with
combinational logic circuits. Most signals from the Instruction Decoder
are applied to control the PLA of the Microinstruction Memory (MIM).
Some signals are applied to the Interrupt Register and the Interface Block.

After processing of the current instruction is completed, the next
instruction is transferred from the IBR to the Instruction Register (IR).
From the IR, the instruction code is sent to the MIM.

The MIM is implemented as a PLA containing 200 logic product terms.
The MIM PLA generates the sequence of microinstructions that provides
operand address generation, instruction fetch and execution, and
interrupt processing.

The Next Address Register (NAR) is used to transition from the current
microinstruction to the next one. The next address is generated during
execution of the current microinstruction and, before execution of the
next microinstruction, is copied into the Current Address Register (CAR).
When generating the first microinstruction, the CAR is loaded with the
starting address from the Instruction Decoder.

Interrupt codes are supplied from the Interrupt Register to the
Interrupt Register (INTR). For software interrupts, the INTR is loaded
under microprogram control using a special microinstruction format.

A branch condition signal is also applied to the input of the MIM PLA.
This signal is generated during execution of branch instructions and in
certain special cases.

The microinstruction code generated by the MIM PLA is written into the
Microinstruction Register (MIR). In addition to the microinstruction,
the MIM PLA generates a number of control flags. These include the
signals "Accept Interrupt (AI)", "Wait State (WS)", "End of Instruction
(EI)", and several others.

The operation of the MCU and its synchronization with other blocks is
controlled by the MCU Synchronization Block (MCU-SYNC).

If no wait signals are present, the MCU-SYNC is started by the
Operational Unit Ready (OU Ready) signal.

The MCU may be halted while waiting for instruction acceptance by the
End of Instruction (EI) signal, while waiting for condition-code
generation by the Wait State (WS) signal, and during processing of
certain interrupts by a stall signal from the Interrupt Block (IB)
(TIB).

During execution of a microinstruction, the MCU-SYNC generates the
MCU Ready signal, which starts the Operational Unit Synchronization
Block (OU-SYNC).

If execution of a microinstruction is delayed, the MCU-SYNC remains
stopped until the OU Ready signal is received.

5.5. Branch Condition Processing Block

The structural diagram of the Branch Condition Processing Block (BCPB)
is shown in Figure 11.

The BCPB is intended to generate the Branch Control Signal (BCS) used
to control the MCU on the basis of the instruction operation code and
the branch condition flags N, Z, V, and C generated in the Operational
Unit during instruction execution.

The BCPB consists of the following blocks and registers:
    Instruction Register (IR);
    Processor Status Register (PSR);
    PLA consisting of two matrices M1 and M2;
    BCPB Synchronization Block.

The instruction code (bits 8–15) is loaded into the IR whenever an
instruction is received.

After completion of each instruction, and during execution of certain
instructions, the condition flags N, Z, V, and C are written into the
PSR.

Information from these registers is supplied to the input of the first
PLA matrix.

Based on the instruction code and processor status, the BCPB PLA
generates the branch condition signal.

The operation of the Branch Condition Processing Block (BCPB) is controlled
by the BCPB Synchronization Block (BCPB-SYNC).

The BCPB-SYNC is started whenever any instruction is written into the
MCU Instruction Register by the SUV signal, and when the "Wait State"
condition appears, by the PS signal.

If the branch condition is generated in response to the "Wait State"
signal, then after completion of the BCPB cycle a KPS signal is generated,
which starts the MCU and removes the stall caused by the "Wait State"
condition.

5.6. Interrupt Block
The structural diagram of the Interrupt Block (IB) is shown in Figure 12.

The Interrupt Block is used for reception and preliminary processing of
interrupt signals. The IB also contains the hardware logic required to
support execution of the RESET instruction.

The IB consists of the following blocks:
    Interrupt Source Register (ISR);
    PLA implemented with matrices M1 and M2;
    9-bit Counter (CNT);
    Control Unit (CU);
    Synchronization Block (IB-SYNC).

All interrupt signals are applied to the Interrupt Source Register.

When executing the WAIT instruction, the "Wait" flip-flop in the ISR is
set under microprogram control using a special microinstruction format.

From the ISR, interrupt signals are applied to the inputs of the first
PLA matrix. An interrupt priority scheme is implemented in the PLA.

Each interrupt has its own priority. If two interrupts are asserted
simultaneously, the interrupt with the higher priority is serviced first.

If bit 7 of the Processor Status Register (PSR) is set to one, external
non-fatal interrupts are masked.

In addition to implementing the interrupt priority scheme, the Interrupt
Block PLA generates the Interrupt Vector Address (IVA) for fetching the
interrupt vector from the Constant Block of the Operational Unit, and
the Interrupt Code (IC), which is used to switch the MCU to the interrupt
service microprogram.

A 9-bit counter is used for detecting bus hangs and for generating the
INIT signal during execution of the RESET instruction.

The counter is started by the DIN or DOUT signal when monitoring bus
hang conditions, or under microprogram control during execution of the
RESET instruction.

The Control Unit monitors when the counter reaches the required state.
The Control Unit also generates a reset signal (returning all processor
blocks to their initial state) and, in certain cases, a signal that
stalls the MCU.

Operation of the Interrupt Block is controlled by the Interrupt Block
Synchronization Unit (IB-SYNC). It is started by the "AI" (Accept
Interrupt) signal from the MCU.

The IVA and IC codes are written into their respective destination
registers by the "Interrupt Ready" signal.

5.7. Interface Block

The structural diagram of the Interface Block (IB) is shown in Figure 13.

The Interface Block is intended to organize transfers between the
processor and devices on the system bus. The Interface Block also
contains the Direct Memory Access (DMA) arbiter.

The Interface Block consists of the following units:
    DMA Arbiter (DMAA);
    Address Output Block (AOB);
    Data Input/Output Block (DIOB);
    Microinstruction Exchange Field Decoder (MEFD);
    Transfer Control Logic (TCL).

The DMA Arbiter is intended to provide Direct Memory Access operation
for devices connected to the system bus of a computer built around the
processor.

The DMA Arbiter monitors incoming DMA requests. After a request is
received, the processor completes the current system bus transaction and
grants DMA access. During the DMA cycle, processor operation is halted.

After an address has been calculated and written into the Address
Register (AR), an exchange request is sent to the Interface Block.

If the system bus is free, the Address Output Block (AOB) begins
placing the address onto the system bus.

After the address has been issued, control is transferred to the
Data Input/Output Block (DIOB), and, depending on the microinstruction
exchange code, a data read cycle, data write cycle, or instruction fetch
cycle is performed.

If the exchange is non-addressed (interrupt vector fetch or reading the
processor status register), the exchange request is processed directly
by the DIOB. In this case, the AOB is not activated.

The microinstruction exchange code is supplied to the Exchange Field
Decoder (EFD). This decoder generates signals that determine the type
of exchange, the direction of transfer, and several auxiliary control
flags.

Synchronization of the individual Interface Block units and coordination
between the Interface Block and the other processor units is performed
by the Transfer Control Logic (TCL).

The TCL receives the signals "Write Address Register" (WAR) and
"Write Data Register" (WDR), indicating that the address and data are
ready for output.

In turn, the TCL generates signals for writing into the Instruction
Buffer Register (IBR) and Data Register (DR) when instructions or data
are received from the system bus.

If data arrival from the system bus is delayed, the TCL generates
stall signals for the Operational Unit.

The timing diagrams for external bus transactions are described in the
next chapter.

6. DESCRIPTION OF PROCESSOR OPERATION

6.1. Processor Operation

The microprocessor is a complete functional module.

In a computer of minimal configuration, only appropriately organized
memory is required for its operation.

However, the processor provides means for interface adjustment that make
it possible to modify interface timing diagrams with the aid of external
circuits, adapting them to specific application requirements.

The processor also provides the possibility of extending the instruction
set by implementing additional instructions in system (hidden) memory.

The processor contains facilities for organizing system memory in such a
way that its address space does not overlap with the addresses of the
computer's main memory.

System memory supplements main memory and is accessible only through
special instructions.

The processor implements an instruction prefetch mechanism.

The instruction fetch and execution algorithm is arranged so that by the
time execution of the current instruction is completed, the next
instruction has already been fetched into the Instruction Buffer
Register, and fetching of yet another instruction has begun.

Naturally, such prefetching is possible only in linear sections of a
program where no branches occur.

When executing branch instructions, and in general any instructions that
load the Program Counter, the instruction already fetched into the
Instruction Buffer Register is no longer the instruction expected by the
program.

In such cases, the correct next instruction is fetched again by hardware.

To restore the prefetch pipeline, the same instruction prepares...

To restore the prefetch pipeline, the same instruction prepares the fetching of one more instruction is initiated. Loss of prefetching also occurs when data rather than an instruction is read via the program counter. At the end of an instruction that addresses data through the program counter, prefetching is likewise restored by arranging the reading of the two instructions following the current one.

An instruction is also refetched when the current instruction modifies the instruction that follows it. After completion of the modification procedure, i.e., the write to the address of the next instruction, the modified instruction is read and executed. The instruction must be fetched again because during execution of the current instruction the next instruction had already been received into the Command Buffer Register (BRK).

Every instruction received by the processor is written into the BRK, from which it is sent to the Instruction Decoder. The Instruction Decoder is started when an instruction has been received into the BRK and a flag indicating that the previous instruction has completed is set. By the end of the decoder cycle, the instruction is transferred from the BRK to the Instruction Register (RK), the initial address of the microprogram is loaded into the Current Address Register, certain service flags are set, and the PLA of the Microinstruction Memory is started.

The generated microinstruction is written into the Microinstruction Register (RMK) and is sent to the decoder of the microinstruction read field. After decoding, the Operational Block (OB) is started and the read phase is executed. During execution of the read phase, the write field of the microinstruction is decoded, and after completion of the read phase the write phase is executed.

While the Operational Block is running, the Microprogram Control Unit (BMU) generates the next microinstruction. This process of microinstruction generation and execution continues until execution of the instruction is completed.

In the penultimate microinstruction, the Interrupt Block (BPR) is started. If there is an unmasked interrupt (the corresponding code is supplied to the Interrupt Register of the BMU), the processor switches to the interrupt-handling microprogram of interrupt handling.

Every instruction involves access to devices on the system bus. These accesses include fetching the next instruction and reading or writing data. If the exchange field of a microinstruction contains an indication that access to the system bus is required, the Operational Block (OB) generates a bus request signal, which is sent to the Interface Block (IB).

If the system bus is free, the IB performs the bus transaction. During this time the OB may execute microinstructions that are not related to the exchange operation or that prepare for the next exchange. After processing the current instruction is completed, the processor proceeds to the next instruction, and so on until the end of the program.

The following sections describe in detail all types of processor exchanges over the system bus.

6.2. General Principles of Interface Organization and Explanation of Timing Diagrams

The processor uses an asynchronous method for address output and data transfer.

By driving the SYNC signal low, the processor informs devices on the system bus that an address has been placed on the AD(0:15) lines. The address is not removed and the exchange procedure does not continue until a low level appears on the AR input of the processor.

During a data read operation, by driving the DIN signal low, the processor informs external devices that the address output phase has been completed and that it is ready to receive data. The read procedure does not continue until a low level appears on the RPLY input.

The indication that data reception has completed is the return of the DIN output to the high level.

During a write operation, the indication that the processor has placed data on the AD(0:15) lines is the assertion of the signal (low level) on the output DOUT.

The write operation does not continue until a low level appears on the RPLY signal. The indication that the write operation has completed is the return of the DOUT output of the processor to the high level.

The processor begins a bus transaction only when the system bus is free. For the processor, the indication that the system bus is free is the presence of high levels on the SACK, AR, and RPLY signals.

If it is necessary to stop the processor during operation, it is best to use the DMR signal. When this signal is driven low, the processor completes the current bus transaction and then stops. When the DMR signal returns to the high level, the processor resumes execution of the program from the point at which it stopped.

The DMR, AR, and RPLY signals are synchronized to the processor's internal clock. The internal synchronization signal is available on the CLCO pin. The frequency of the internal synchronization clock is one-half of the external synchronization frequency supplied to the CLCI input.

The RPLY signal is sampled by the processor during the high phase of the CLCO signal, while the DMR signal is sampled during the low phase of CLCO.

The AR signal during address output (low level) is sampled during the low phase of CLCO. The transition of AR to the high level is recognized by the processor during the high phase of CLCO.

When the processor operates with fast external devices, for example RAM located on the same board as the processor, maximum performance is achieved when generation of the AR and RPLY signals is coordinated with the moments at which they are sampled by the processor.

The DMR and SACK signals are used only during the direct-memory-access (DMA) control transfer procedure and have little effect on overall system performance.

The SACK signal is accepted by the processor asynchronously. The end of the SACK signal (high level) is recognized by the processor during the high phase of the CLCO signal.

The duration of the address output phase during an addressed bus transaction is controlled by the AR signal. To make this phase as short as possible, the AR signal must be driven low no later than 50 ns before the beginning of the positive edge of the CLCO pulse following the pulse during which the SYNC signal is generated. If this requirement is met, the processor, after some delay relative to the transition of AR from high to low, removes the address from the AD pins (placing these pins into the high-impedance state during a read operation).

For all types of addressed bus transactions, completion of the current bus cycle and transition to the next cycle occur in the same manner. Upon receiving the RPLY signal (low level), the processor performs the read or write operation and removes its DIN, DOUT, and SYNC signals regardless of when the RPLY signal subsequently returns to the high level.

If, during the current bus cycle, the processor has generated a request for the next bus cycle and there is no DMA request, then the start of the next bus transaction depends only on the state of the AR signal (it is desirable that AR be released before SYNC is removed) and does not depend on the state of the RPLY signal. In this case, the processor will place the address for the next bus cycle on the bus simultaneously with the removal of the SYNC signal.

If the processor did not generate a request for the next bus transaction during the current bus cycle, or if a DMA request arrived during this time, then the start of the next bus cycle depends not only on the state of AR, but also on the state of the RPLY signal level (either from its own current transaction or from another transaction if DMA occurred). In this case, the beginning of the next bus cycle requires both RPLY and AR to be at the high level.

Also, if the AR signal is released later than one CLCO period after the removal of the SYNC signal, then the next bus transaction will begin only after both AR and RPLY have returned to the high level.

After the interrupt vector address reception procedure, the start of the processor’s next cycle unconditionally depends on the states of the AR and RPLY signals. To delay the restart of the processor, it is recommended to use only the AR signal. During interrupt vector address reception, the AR signal may be generated from the RPLY signal.

If the processor exchanges data with slow external devices, the timing diagram of the processor interface signals can be modified by means of external circuitry. In this case, permission to begin the next bus cycle must be supplied to the processor by means of ...

[Handwritten note]

When operating with fast memory at a high clock frequency, the following is recommended to achieve maximum performance:

When reading instructions or data, immediately remove the RPLY signal as soon as the DIN signal is removed during the low phase of the CLCO signal; otherwise, in the subsequent addressed transaction there will be a delay in asserting DIN for an address read cycle or a delay in outputting data during a write cycle.

The processor reaction time to removal of the RPLY signal does not exceed 1.5·TCLCO, provided that the RPLY signal is removed no later than the beginning of the high phase of the CLCO signal.
